subject: Example of a model that can't be represented by a directed acyclic graph?

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Example of a model that can't be represented by a directed acyclic graph?
parts:
Hi all,

I know the language allows for more flexibility than probabilistic models built up with a directed acyclic graph. I know that functions are one example of a language construct that destroys the guarantee of DAG, but I was wondering if there's a simple example of a model that can't be written with a DAG.


Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Example of a model that can't be represented by a directed acyclic graph?
parts:
It depends what you mean by written as a DAG.

Any time you have to write out a custom density, you
can't do that directly with a DAG. But BUGS/JAGS lets you
hack it by using what they call the zeros trick. If you want
to add log(phi) to the log density, you can do this:

z <- 0
z ~ dpois(phi)

That means you can technically marginalize out nuisance
parameters, but the code's going to be ugly.

Any time you want to write an iterative algorithm,
you can't do that directly with a DAG. Usually that's
to add a new function or a new density; if you can
keep adding to the building blocks of the DAG language,
then there's a lot more you can do.

Spline models can't easily be coded up using DAGs.
BUGS builds in an interpolate function, but it's fixed
in its behavior.

More generally, any if-then block with a complex body
is not a graphical model. I think you can hack this in JAGS/BUGS
with a combination of ifelse and the zeros trick.

In the limit, if you have a model with a likelihood

y ~ foo(theta);

and prior

theta ~ bar();

then if you code up a multivariate probability function foo and
multivariate prior distribution bar, you can represent it
graphically as above. Stan just makes it easy for you to code up
arbitrary foo() and bar(). A good example of something that'd be
a pain to code in BUGS/JAGS would be the forward-backward algorithm
for HMMs. You use those for chained conditional random fields, a
kind of Markov random field for tagging sequences. While I think
you could do it with a lot of global variables and the Poisson
trick, is what you have left really a graphical model in the sense
that people mean when they talk about graphical models?

It's easy to line-for-line port a JAGS/BUGS program
to Stan, but the other way around is non-trivial.

- Bob
